claims.title: What people are saying
claims.intro: These are the claims about the result that circulate most. Each carries the short answer, the method behind it, and — where one exists — the exact figure that confirms or contradicts it. Two of them cannot be answered with what this site holds, and say so.
claims.openVerdict: Not evaluable with what this site holds

lead.claim: “The pre-count and the scrutiny did not match.”
lead.answer: The pre-count is an informational transmission with no legal effect; the scrutiny is the count with legal value, and it finishes days later. That the two figures differ is not, by itself, a sign of anything: it is the procedure's intended order. Everything this site publishes about 2026 is pre-count.
lead.method: The layers are kept separate and every figure carries version, source and legal status. A comparison requires the same field, the same table and the same grain.
lead.figureAlt: Six hexagons representing a six-vote difference on a single table
lead.figureNote: Illustration over synthetic data. A real release brings its own figures.

precount.claim: “The tables do not add up to the polling places.”
precount.answer: In the data we hold, each polling place is exactly the sum of its tables: they agree on all five ballot quantities and on the per-candidacy votes. That confirms our copy faithfully reproduces what was published; it says nothing about whether those figures are correct against the paper form.
precount.method: Polling-place and table records compared by their parent link, in both rounds. Exact agreement is expected when the place is the aggregate the server itself computes over the tables.

metadata.claim: “The E-14 forms come out with no metadata.”
metadata.answer: The 2026 E-14s we examined carry no document-information dictionary and no cryptographic signature. That is a real traceability gap: the file cannot attest its own origin. It is not proof that anything was altered, and a change of toolchain between elections explains it without supposing anything was removed.
metadata.method: One hundred documents read with a PDF parser, against a positive control. What we did not measure: the 2022 E-14s, whose portal is no longer reachable, so we cannot date the change.

coverage.answer: The scrutiny channel declares 118,350 tables scrutinised at 100%. That is the national count minus the 3,670 consular tables, which that channel does not include by design: the scrutiny architecture has no commission for the exterior. A 100% from that channel covers the domestic count only, whoever states it.
coverage.method: Document index for both rounds: 33 department codes, no code 88 (Consulados). Historical contrast: in 2018 there were published actas from the exterior, so this is a reversible gap, not a constant.

hash.claim: “The file code does not verify integrity.”
hash.answer: In the channel we examined, the code inside the filename is not a fingerprint of its content: it is four characters, it repeats across documents, and the same name appears in both rounds naming two different documents. Such a value cannot verify integrity.
hash.method: 118,343 first-round references: every code four characters, 2,743 distinct values, one shared by 76 documents. We did not test the citizen-viewer channel, where a different code is generated.

transcription.claim: “The published numbers match what is written on the actas.”
transcription.answer: Nothing on this site compares a published figure to the number handwritten on the corresponding E-14. That is the link that would settle the point, and it requires reading the forms: we did not.

twentytwo.claim: “In 2022 the E-14s kept metadata and in 2026 they do not.”
twentytwo.answer: We cannot answer it. The 2022 documents were served behind an anti-automation control with no direct links, so they were never archived and are not reachable by any legitimate route from here.

comparison.title: Was 2026 a strange election?
comparison.introA: The only way to answer that is to measure 2018 and 2022 with the same code and look at all three together. You will never see the 2026 number alone here, because a number alone means nothing.

thermometer.lead: These tests produce numbers that are alarming even in perfectly clean elections.
thermometer.body: It is like a temperature. 37.2 is alarming until you learn the person next to you read 38.5 and was healthy. That is why 2026 always appears beside 2018 and 2022, measured with the same thermometer.

legend.1: Each test compares 2026 against the range of values already seen in 2018 and 2022.
legend.2: All three elections are measured with the same code, so none of them carries more weight than the others.
legend.3: If 2026 falls within what was already seen, it resembles the earlier elections. If it falls outside, it is flagged for human review — never as a conclusion.

benford.label: What about Benford's law, which fails in all three?
benford.box: there is nothing to compare here
benford.body: This test is not built for counting votes: mesas vary too widely in size, and that breaks it. It fails in all three elections, even the ones nobody disputes. It is still published, because hiding it would look worse — but no band is drawn for it here, because comparing it would not mean anything.

comparison.footnote: The concrete figures for each test are published in the methodology, with their code, so anyone can recompute them. Here the comparison matters, not the isolated value.

process.title: How a vote reaches this page
process.intro: Nine steps between the official document and what you see above. Three of them are gates: if they are not cleared, nothing is published, not even partially. The site prefers to say nothing over saying something it cannot support.

01.title: Retrieval
01.body: The official object is downloaded and stored with its hash and timestamp.

02.title: Normalisation
02.body: It is parsed to a fixed schema, keeping the source's raw value.

03.title: Reconciliation
03.body: Every aggregate must match its parts exactly, or it stops.

04.title: Coverage
04.body: What was and was not collected is recorded, without filling the gaps.

05.title: Statistical validation
05.body: Quality controls must pass before anything is exposed.

06.title: Neutral wording
06.body: A gate rejects any language that would imply a conclusion.

07.title: Immutable versioning
07.body: The release is frozen with its hash; a rollback is a pointer change.

08.title: Independent audit
08.body: An external review must accept the release before it is activated.

09.title: Publication
09.body: Only then does the public pointer change. Today it points to synthetic data.

log.title: How it was built
log.intro: The order in which decisions were taken matters as much as the result. Several — separating the layers, not filling the gaps, excluding Benford — were taken before the 2026 data was seen, which is why they hold up afterward.
log.trackHint: Scroll horizontally with a mouse, trackpad, or the arrow keys.

layers.title: Separate the layers
layers.body: Pre-count, documentary evidence and scrutiny are kept apart; none silently replaces another.

sentinel.title: Empty is not zero
sentinel.body: An unavailable value never becomes a zero. It is the rule that most often prevented an error, including our own.

benford.title: Do not use Benford
benford.body: Benford's law is invalid for vote counts with heterogeneous table sizes; it was excluded from the start.

indexonly.title: Index-only for the E-14s
indexonly.body: The actas are not downloaded, OCR'd or derived: the official reference is kept. The forms carry signatures and ID numbers.

retraction.title: Retract a finding
retraction.body: A result about the overseas vote was published and then withdrawn: measured across all 34 departments, it did not hold. The full retraction is on record.

data.title: Where it all comes from
data.intro: Everything above comes from three files and an OpenAPI contract. Each version is immutable and travels with its hash, so anyone can recompute the result without asking permission.
